Jackson's former nurse, Cherilyn Lee, was also approached on Wednesday by investigators who wanted copies of medical files she had on the singer, Lee told CNN's Nancy Grace. Lee said she handed over the files to officials with the coroner's office. Ed Chernoff, a Houston lawyer hired by Murray soon after Jackson's death, confirmed that Los Angeles Police detectives and federal Drug Enforcement Administration agents used a search warrant to enter Murray's office in northeast Houston on Wednesday morning. "The search warrant authorized law enforcement to search for and seize items, including documents, they believed constituted evidence of the offense of manslaughter," Chernoff said in a written statement Wednesday. Chernoff said members of Murray's legal team were at the medical office during the search, which he said "was conducted by members of the DEA, two robbery-homicide detectives from the Los Angeles Police Department and Houston Police officers." "Law enforcement concluded their search around 12:30 p.m. and left with a forensic image of a business computer hard drive and 21 documents. None of the documents taken had previously been requested by law enforcement or the L.A. coroner's office," Chernoff said. Tammy Kidd, a spokeswoman at Chernoff's office, said the search "was absolutely a surprise to us, because we've had open lines of communication this whole time." "Based on Dr. Murray's minute-by-minute and item-by-item description of Michael Jackson's last days, he should not be a target of criminal charges," Chernoff said Tuesday. "Dr. Murray was the last doctor standing when Michael Jackson died and it seems all the fury is directed toward him." Los Angeles investigators have interviewed Murray twice, Chernoff said. A third interview has not been scheduled, he said. Police impounded his car, which had been parked at Jackson's Holmby Hills home, the night after Jackson's death. It was released to Murray several days later. "Dr. Murray is frustrated by negative and often erroneous media reports. He has to walk around 24-7 with a bodyguard," Chernoff said. "He can't operate his practice. He can't go to work because he is harassed no matter where he goes." At least two investigations are under way into Jackson's death. The Los Angeles County coroner is waiting for toxicology results to determine a cause of death, while the city Police Department, with assistance from the Drug Enforcement Administration, is looking at the possibility of criminal charges. A coroner's office spokesman said the autopsy findings could be released in the next week or more. Los Angeles Police Chief William Bratton told CNN he would wait for the coroner to determine the exact cause of Jackson's death. "And based on those, we will have an idea of what it is we are dealing (with): Are we dealing with a homicide, or are we dealing with an accidental overdose?" he said. CNN's Alan Duke, Ted Rowlands and Randi Kaye contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Texas authorities on Thursday released court documents detailing items seized from the medical office and storage unit of Dr. Conrad Murray, the cardiologist who was with Michael Jackson when the singer fell ill and died on June 25.

According to court documents, detectives searched both locations in Houston on Wednesday for “evidence of the offense of manslaughter.” Murray’s attorney confirmed the search that same day.

Among the items removed from Murray’s office were a computer; 27 tablets of Phentermine, a prescription-strength appetite suppressant; one tablet of clonazepam, an anti-anxiety medication; and several Rolodex cards. From Murray’s storage unit, authorities removed two computer hard drives; an “important contact list”; a suspension notice from Houston’s Doctors Hospital; notices from the Internal Revenue Service; and a list of medical and hospital documents.

Jackson’s former nurse, Cherilyn Lee, was also approached Wednesday by investigators seeking copies of medical files she had on the singer, Lee told CNN’s Nancy Grace. Lee said she turned the files over to officials with the coroner’s office.

Ed Chernoff, a Houston attorney retained by Murray shortly after Jackson’s death, confirmed that Los Angeles Police detectives and federal Drug Enforcement Administration agents used a search warrant to enter Murray’s office in northeast Houston on Wednesday morning.

“The search warrant authorized law enforcement to search for and seize items, including documents, they believed constituted evidence of the offense of manslaughter,” Chernoff said in a written statement Wednesday.

Chernoff said members of Murray’s legal team were present at the medical office during the search, which he said “was conducted by members of the DEA, two robbery-homicide detectives from the Los Angeles Police Department and Houston Police officers.”

“Law enforcement concluded their search around 12:30 p.m. and left with a forensic image of a business computer hard drive and 21 documents. None of the documents taken had previously been requested by law enforcement or the L.A. coroner’s office,” Chernoff said.

Tammy Kidd, a spokeswoman at Chernoff’s office, said the search “was absolutely a surprise to us, because we’ve had open lines of communication this whole time.”

“Based on Dr. Murray’s minute-by-minute and item-by-item description of Michael Jackson’s last days, he should not be a target of criminal charges,” Chernoff said Tuesday. “Dr. Murray was the last doctor standing when Michael Jackson died and it seems all the fury is directed toward him.”

Los Angeles investigators have interviewed Murray twice, Chernoff said. A third interview has not been scheduled, he added. Police impounded Murray’s car, which had been parked at Jackson’s Holmby Hills home, the night after Jackson’s death. It was released to Murray several days later.

“Dr. Murray is frustrated by negative and often erroneous media reports. He has to walk around 24-7 with a bodyguard,” Chernoff said. “He can’t operate his practice. He can’t go to work because he is harassed no matter where he goes.”

At least two investigations into Jackson’s death are under way. The Los Angeles County coroner is awaiting toxicology results to determine the cause of death, while the city Police Department, with assistance from the Drug Enforcement Administration, is examining the possibility of criminal charges.

A coroner’s office spokesman said the autopsy findings could be released within the next week or more.

Los Angeles Police Chief William Bratton told CNN he would wait for the coroner to determine the exact cause of Jackson’s death.

“And based on those, we will have an idea of what it is we are dealing [with]: Are we dealing with a homicide, or are we dealing with an accidental overdose?” he said.

CNN’s Alan Duke, Ted Rowlands and Randi Kaye contributed to this report.

Investigators also sought evidence related to anesthetic and sedative drugs, including propofol — the powerful anesthetic later identified by the Los Angeles County coroner as a key factor in Jackson’s death.

According to the released documents, investigators searched Murray’s Armstrong Medical Clinic in Houston and a storage unit connected to him as part of a broader effort to reconstruct Jackson’s medical care. The warrants indicate authorities were looking for records of medications obtained, stored or administered, as well as documents that could establish timelines, communications and treatment decisions.

## Breaking News Report: Search Warrants Executed at Dr. Conrad Murray’s Offices in Michael Jackson Death Investigation

**HOUSTON / LOS ANGELES —** Law enforcement authorities investigating the death of Michael Jackson executed search warrants at medical offices connected to **Dr. Conrad Murray**, the personal physician who was with the pop star in the hours before his death, as detectives intensified a probe that court records indicated was focused on possible **manslaughter**.

The searches, carried out by investigators from the **Los Angeles Police Department** with assistance from federal agents, targeted Murray’s medical practice as authorities sought records and evidence related to medications administered to Jackson before he was pronounced dead on **June 25, 2009**, at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center.

### Warrants Sought Evidence in Manslaughter Probe

According to warrant materials and statements from officials at the time, investigators were looking for evidence connected to the possible improper administration of powerful sedatives and anesthetics, including **propofol**, a hospital-grade anesthetic that later became central to the criminal investigation.

Search warrant affidavits described the inquiry as involving potential **manslaughter**, reflecting investigators’ focus on whether Jackson’s death resulted from gross negligence or improper medical treatment.

Dr. Murray, a cardiologist, had been hired to care for Jackson as the entertainer prepared for his planned **“This Is It”** concert residency in London. Murray was present at Jackson’s rented Holmby Hills mansion when Jackson became unresponsive.

### Items Seized From Murray’s Office

During the search of Murray’s office in Houston, investigators seized a range of materials believed to be relevant to Jackson’s treatment and Murray’s medical practice.

Items reported seized included:

- **Medical records and patient files**
- **Computer hard drives and digital storage media**
- **E-mails and correspondence**
- **Appointment records**
- **Prescription-related documents**
- **Billing and financial records**
- **Medication-related materials**
- Other documents tied to Murray’s treatment of Michael Jackson

Authorities were particularly interested in establishing what drugs had been obtained, prescribed, or administered to Jackson, and whether proper medical standards had been followed.

Additional searches were also conducted at locations associated with Murray, including his **Las Vegas office and residence**, as investigators traced drug purchases, medical supplies, and records linked to Jackson’s final weeks.

### Focus on Propofol and Sedatives

The investigation centered on Jackson’s use of medications to treat chronic insomnia. Reports at the time said investigators were examining Murray’s role in administering **propofol**, along with other sedatives such as **lorazepam** and **midazolam**.

Propofol is typically used in operating rooms and clinical settings under close monitoring because it can suppress breathing and requires specialized equipment and trained personnel. Its presence in Jackson’s home became one of the most significant issues in the case.

Investigators sought to determine:

- Who supplied the drugs
- How they were transported and stored
- Whether Murray administered them
- Whether proper monitoring equipment was present
- Whether emergency response was delayed
- Whether Jackson’s death was preventable

### Attorney: Murray Cooperating With Authorities

Dr. Murray’s attorney, **Ed Chernoff**, said Murray was cooperating with investigators and maintained that the doctor had not given Jackson anything that should have caused his death.

Chernoff stated that Murray had voluntarily spoken with police and provided information about Jackson’s final hours. He also emphasized that Murray was not attempting to hide from authorities and had been assisting the investigation.

At the time of the searches, Chernoff objected to any suggestion that Murray was criminally responsible, saying the doctor cared deeply about Jackson and was devastated by his death.

Murray’s legal team repeatedly maintained that he did not “prescribe or administer anything that should have killed Michael Jackson,” while acknowledging that investigators were examining the medical care provided in the singer’s final hours.

### Jackson’s Final Hours Under Scrutiny

Michael Jackson died after suffering cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles mansion. Emergency responders arrived after a 911 call was placed from the home, and Jackson was transported to UCLA Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.

Detectives later scrutinized the timeline of events, including:

- When Jackson became unresponsive
- What medications were given that morning
- Whether Murray attempted resuscitation properly
- Why emergency services were not contacted sooner
- Whether medical equipment in the home was adequate

The search warrants were viewed as a major escalation in the investigation, shifting attention from a general death inquiry to a potential criminal case.

### Coroner’s Finding and Criminal Case

The Los Angeles County coroner later ruled Jackson’s death a **homicide**, caused primarily by **acute propofol intoxication**, with other sedatives contributing.

Dr. Conrad Murray was ultimately charged with **involuntary manslaughter**. Prosecutors argued that he acted with gross negligence by administering propofol in a home setting without proper safeguards and by failing to appropriately monitor Jackson.

Murray denied criminal wrongdoing, but in 2011 he was convicted of involuntary manslaughter and sentenced to four years in jail. He served roughly two years before being released due to jail overcrowding and good behavior credits.

### Significance of the Office Searches

The search warrants executed at Murray’s offices marked a pivotal moment in the investigation into Michael Jackson’s death. The records and materials seized helped investigators reconstruct Jackson’s medical treatment, trace drug procurement, and build the case around the use of propofol outside a hospital setting.

The raids also made clear that authorities were no longer treating Jackson’s death solely as a medical tragedy, but as a potential criminal act involving the conduct of his personal physician.

Prosecutors later alleged Murray acted with gross negligence by administering the drug in a home setting without adequate safeguards and by failing to properly monitor Jackson or quickly summon emergency help.

Murray was charged with involuntary manslaughter in 2010. He pleaded not guilty, but was convicted in 2011 and sentenced to four years in jail. He served about two years before being released.
